screens.title: Designing Engaging User Interfaces & HUDs
screens.narratorSegment: As you approach the final polish on a Roblox game, the way you present information and controls becomes central to player enjoyment. A good user interface does more than look nice; it communicates state, reduces confusion, and enables players to take the right action quickly. In this lesson you will learn the main building blocks of Roblox UI—ScreenGui, Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, and ImageLabel—how to organize them for clarity, and how to make them responsive across devices using UDim2 and AnchorPoint. We'll also practice a simple HUD that shows health, score, and a toggled shop panel using a local script for client-side interaction. Along the way, you will see common pitfalls such as relying only on pixel offsets or failing to group elements into Frames, and learn how to avoid them. By the end, you should be able to create modular, testable UI that adapts to different devices and gives players the information they need without clutter. Think about one interface in your favorite game and how it keeps you informed—that is the standard we aim for here.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Designing UIs & HUDs
Designing Engaging User Interfaces & HUDs
Create interfaces that communicate player state clearly, adapt to different screens, and connect to game logic with local scripts for responsive interaction.
Why this chapter matters
Players judge polish by how easily they can read health, score, and controls. Clear UI keeps players engaged and reduces churn.
Hands-on orientation

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll build four practical UI skills that are core to Roblox game polish. First, you'll understand the role of UI and UX: why thoughtful layout, labels, and feedback determine whether a player stays or leaves. We will explain what qualifies as UI versus UX, and give a simple example of a health indicator that both looks good and communicates state quickly. Second, you'll identify and use core Roblox UI elements such as ScreenGui, Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, and ImageLabel. You will learn where to place these objects in the Explorer and why ScreenGui copies to each player's PlayerGui. Third, you'll implement responsive layouts with UDim2, AnchorPoint, Scale and Offset. You will practice a pattern that uses Scale for primary sizing and Offset for minimum pixel adjustments so your UI looks consistent across monitors and phones. Fourth, you will develop interactive UI and wire it to game logic with a LocalScript listening for MouseButton1Click events. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency by building a simple TopBar HUD with a toggled Shop panel.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Practice & Verification
Verification checklist
  • 1. Add ScreenGui to StarterGui and confirm PlayerGui cloning on play-test.
  • 2. Create TopBarFrame with AnchorPoint (0.5,0) and Size using Scale for width and height percentages.
  • 3. Set HealthLabel and ScoreLabel alignment using TextXAlignment and AnchorPoint patterns.
  • 4. Add ShopButton with a LocalScript toggling ShopPanel via MouseButton1Click and test visibility toggles locally.
Common mistakes
Placing interactive UI logic on the server, over-relying on Offset for layout, and failing to use Frames to group related elements are frequent issues. Use this checklist to catch them early.

screens.title: UI vs UX — why both matter
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s define the difference between User Interface and User Experience and why both matter in a Roblox game. User Interface refers to the concrete elements players see and interact with: TextLabels, TextButtons, ImageLabels, Frames, and the ScreenGui container that holds them. User Experience is broader: it is the player's perception of how easy the game is to read, navigate, and interact with. In practice, a UI component like a health bar is a small part of UX: its placement, color contrast, label clarity, and animation together determine whether a player recognizes their low health in time. A concrete example: a small grey numeric health value in a corner can be a UI that fails the UX test because it is hard to scan quickly during gameplay; a bold, high-contrast bar near the top with a numeric overlay is both UI and better UX. A common misconception is to treat UX as only visual polish—UX also includes feedback timing, predictability of controls, and accessibility for different devices. To check your design, ask: can a new player find the health and shop controls within three seconds? If not, iterate until you can. This definition anchors all later screens: we will make UI elements that intentionally support better UX.

keyIdea.title: UI vs UX
keyIdea.text: UI are the visible components; UX is the player's overall ability to use and understand them. Good UI supports good UX through clarity and predictable feedback.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › UI vs UX
Definition and practical test
User Interface = visual elements and controls. User Experience = how intuitively players use those elements. Use quick tests to validate which is which.
Concrete example: a health indicator. UI: a bar and number. UX: placement, contrast, and timing of updates so players react correctly under pressure.
Common misconception
Polish alone doesn't equal good UX. Fancy visuals without clarity still confuse new players. Performance and responsiveness are UX concerns too.
Key Takeaway

Design UI elements that communicate purpose instantly; evaluate them for speed, contrast, and predictability to improve UX.

Analogy
Think of UI as the instrument panel and UX as how easily the pilot reads it under turbulence. Clear grouping and readable labels matter more than decorative elements.
Check your understanding
  • • Can a new player find primary controls within three seconds?
  • • Are interactive elements visually distinct from static text?
  • • Does the UI maintain legibility across small screens?

screens.title: ScreenGui and PlayerGui — per-player UI instances
screens.narratorSegment: ScreenGui is the top-level container for everything a player sees as part of the screen overlay. In Roblox, you design UI inside StarterGui because the engine clones those ScreenGui objects into each player's PlayerGui when they join. That cloning behavior is the reason you can safely create a health display that updates only for a single player without affecting others. A typical architecture is: StarterGui contains a ScreenGui named PlayerHUD; PlayerHUD contains Frames such as TopBarFrame and ShopPanel; inside those Frames you place TextLabels, TextButtons, and ImageLabels. A concrete example: add PlayerHUD in StarterGui, then join Play mode and inspect PlayerGui in Explorer to see the copy. A common mistake is trying to update StarterGui at runtime from a server script to change a player's display; those changes affect the template and not the already cloned PlayerGui instances. If you must change live UIs for connected players, either modify their PlayerGui or use RemoteEvents to instruct clients to update their local UI. Always prefer LocalScripts for client-side UI behavior because LocalScripts have access to LocalPlayer and run smoothly on the client. For verification, create a small ScreenGui with a TextLabel that shows the player's name using a LocalScript and see it appear per-player.

keyIdea.title: ScreenGui architecture
keyIdea.text: StarterGui is a template; ScreenGui copies into each player's PlayerGui. Use LocalScripts for per-player UI updates and RemoteEvents when the server must notify clients.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › ScreenGui Architecture
Typical hierarchy
StarterGui → ScreenGui (PlayerHUD) → Frame (TopBarFrame, ShopPanel) → Elements (TextLabel, TextButton, ImageLabel).
Why per-player instances matter
Each player needs their own copy so Personal values like health and inventory update locally without cross-player interference. This avoids accidental global changes.
LocalScript vs Script
LocalScripts run on the client and can access LocalPlayer. Use LocalScripts for UI toggles and animations; use server Scripts for authoritative game state and then inform clients via RemoteEvents.
Quick verification code (LocalScript inside PlayerHUD)
local player = game.Players.LocalPlayer
local gui = script.Parent
local nameLabel = gui:WaitForChild("TopBarFrame"):WaitForChild("PlayerNameLabel")

nameLabel.Text = "Player: " .. player.Name
Common mistake
Modifying StarterGui from the server after players have joined will not update existing PlayerGui copies. Use RemoteEvents to tell clients to update their own GUIs instead.
Pro tip

Name Frames and elements clearly and keep groups together so LocalScripts can find siblings with :WaitForChild reliably.

screens.title: Frames: grouping, layout, and manageability
screens.narratorSegment: Frames are the basic containers you will use to group related UI elements. Think of Frames as panels: they provide a background, a local coordinate space, and a place to apply layout rules. When you put health and score elements inside a TopBarFrame, you can move, scale, or set visibility for the whole group with one property change. That modularity makes it easier to show or hide complex UI states like opening an inventory or toggling a shop panel. A concrete practice: create a TopBarFrame with AnchorPoint set to 0.5 on the X axis and UDim2. new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0) for Size. Inside it, place HealthLabel and ScoreLabel and set their AnchorPoints so alignment remains stable. A common error is placing many elements directly under ScreenGui without Frames, which leads to messy hierarchies and fragile scripts. Another useful technique is to use simple layout objects like UIListLayout or UIPadding inside Frames to maintain spacing when the screen size changes. For example, UIListLayout can ensure buttons stack and scale predictably when the frame resizes. End with this mental check: if you need to toggle, move, or style a set of elements together, put them in a Frame first.

keyIdea.title: Frame usage
keyIdea.text: Group related elements inside Frames to control visibility, movement, and style collectively; use layout objects for spacing and resilience across screen sizes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Frames & Layout
Frame as a container
Frames let you group related UI and apply a single transform, size, or visibility toggle to the entire group. This reduces script complexity and helps keep the Explorer organized.
Example TopBarFrame
AnchorPoint = (0.5, 0), Position = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0, 0), Size = UDim2.new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0). Inside: HealthLabel, ScoreLabel.
Use layout objects
UIListLayout and UIPadding help maintain spacing when the parent frame resizes, avoiding manual repositioning of every child element.
Key Takeaway

Frames make UI modular. Group any elements that change together and leverage layout objects to scale gracefully across screens.

Practical scenario
If you want to show a ShopPanel, put the shop's header, item list, and close button in one Frame and toggle that Frame's Visible property. This avoids searching for scattered children in scripts.
Layout snippet (UIListLayout)
-- Inside a Frame named ItemList
local layout = Instance.new("UIListLayout")
layout.Padding = UDim.new(0, 8)
layout.FillDirection = Enum.FillDirection.Vertical
layout.Parent = script.Parent

screens.title: TextLabel, TextButton, ImageLabel — choosing the right element
screens.narratorSegment: Roblox provides simple building blocks: TextLabel for static text, TextButton for clickable text-based controls, ImageLabel for non-interactive images, and ImageButton when the image should be clickable. Choose the right element to match both behavior and accessibility. For example, use TextLabel for a persistent 'Health:' label. Use TextButton for an interactive 'Shop' control that players click to open a panel. An ImageLabel is great for icons such as a heart or coin, but if the icon should open an inventory, use an ImageButton instead. A concrete design decision: prefer readable fonts and sufficient text size. The chapter recommends TextScaled and a bold font for score and health numbers so they remain legible on small devices. A common beginner mistake is mixing too many styles—different fonts, colors, and button shapes—that makes interactive elements indistinguishable from decorative ones. Maintain consistent visual feedback for interactive elements: slightly darker background on pressed state or a small scale animation improves clarity. Finally, avoid placing sensitive information like server debug text in visible labels. Sanitize any player-supplied text before showing it in TextLabels to prevent confusion or exploitation. As you design, ask whether each element is decorative, informative, or interactive; pick the UI object type that reflects that role.

keyIdea.title: Choose elements by role
keyIdea.text: Use TextLabel/ImageLabel for display-only content and TextButton/ImageButton for interactive controls. Keep fonts, sizes, and feedback consistent to improve clarity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Labels & Buttons
Element roles
TextLabel — display only
Use for non-interactive text like instructions, player names, and labels. Set TextScaled and choose readable fonts for small screens.
TextButton & ImageButton — interactive
Use MouseButton1Click events to trigger LocalScript actions. Provide visual feedback so players know the element is clickable.
Design rule
Keep interactive elements consistent: same corner radius, padding, and color family. Use contrast to separate foreground from background.
Example: Shop button script (LocalScript)
local shopButton = script.Parent
local playerGui = shopButton.Parent
local shopPanel = playerGui:WaitForChild("ShopPanel")

shopButton.MouseButton1Click:Connect(function()
  shopPanel.Visible = not shopPanel.Visible
end)

screens.title: UDim2, Scale vs Offset, and AnchorPoint
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most important technical skills for Roblox UI is mastering UDim2, which combines Scale and Offset to control both size and position. Scale values are fractions of the parent size and make elements resize proportionally. Offset values are fixed pixels used for fine-tuning. A robust pattern is to use Scale for primary sizing and Offset for small adjustments like minimum padding. For example, a TopBarFrame with Size set to UDim2. new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0) will occupy 80 percent of the screen width and 10 percent of the height on any device. AnchorPoint changes the reference point used when positioning an element. By default, position is relative to the top-left corner; setting AnchorPoint to Vector2. new(0.5, 0.5) makes the element center around its assigned Position, which simplifies centering and rotation. A common misconception is that Offset alone is sufficient; a 100-pixel wide button that looks fine on a desktop will be tiny on a phone. To test responsiveness, use Roblox Studio's emulated devices or resize the play window. Below is a concrete code example that demonstrates creating a centered play button that remains 80 percent wide using AnchorPoint and UDim2. Practice by changing Scale and observing how the UI adapts. Final takeaway: prefer Scale for major layout and AnchorPoint for predictable pivots, reserving Offset for minimum pixel spacing.

keyIdea.title: Responsive rules
keyIdea.text: Use UDim2 Scale for proportional sizing, Offset for small pixel tweaks, and AnchorPoint to change the element's pivot for reliable centering.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › UDim2 & AnchorPoint
Scale vs Offset
Scale is proportional and device-agnostic; Offset is fixed pixels. Prefer Scale for primary sizing so UI adapts across phones and monitors.
UDim2 example
-- Centered Play button
button.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)
button.Position = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0)
button.Size = UDim2.new(0.8, 0, 0.2, 0) -- 80% width, 20% height of parent
Common mistake
Using only Offset makes UIs break on different aspect ratios. Test across emulated devices to catch layout breakage early.
Practical checks
  • • Does the element remain readable on the smallest target device?
  • • Does centering remain accurate when the element changes size? If not, adjust AnchorPoint.
  • • Use Offset only to enforce minimum pixel sizes for touch targets.
Key Takeaway

Combine Scale for adaptability with AnchorPoint for reliable pivots; reserve Offset for minor pixel corrections or minimum sizes.

screens.title: LocalScript vs Server Script — where UI logic belongs
screens.narratorSegment: When you build in-game UI, choosing where code runs is one of the most important architecture decisions. A LocalScript runs on the player's device and can update that player's ScreenGui directly. This makes LocalScripts ideal for animations, button handling, and immediate visual feedback. A Server Script runs on the server and controls authoritative game state—things like awarding currency, changing global timers, or updating leaderboards. If you put UI-only code on the server, you either can't directly affect a single player's PlayerGui, or you create lag and security issues. Conversely, putting sensitive logic—like awarding points—only in a LocalScript lets a player spoof results. A common pattern is: LocalScript detects a button click and fires a RemoteEvent to the server; the server validates, updates authoritative state, and informs clients back. Example: the client fires a request to open a shop; the server checks whether purchases are allowed and updates the player's saved balance. Remember to test for nil values and use WaitForChild when querying PlayerGui or replicated objects. A quick misconception check: LocalScripts are not weak—use them for UI—but they are not authoritative. Your takeaway: separate presentation (LocalScript) from game authority (Server Script) and use RemoteEvents to bridge them.

keyIdea.title: Separation of concerns
keyIdea.text: Keep UI presentation in LocalScripts, keep authoritative game state on the server, and bridge them with RemoteEvents for secure interactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Local vs Server
Architecture

Client vs Server Responsibilities

Understand which side owns presentation and which side owns state. View this as a rule: visual and tactile go client; authoritative decisions go server.

Patterns & Calls
  • LocalScript: Button handling, animations, and direct PlayerGui updates.
  • Server Script: Authoritative state changes, awarding currency, saving data to DatastoreService.
  • Bridge: RemoteEvents and validation layers to confirm client requests.
Architecture Diagram

Client ↔ Server flow for a UI action

A compact overview of the handoff when a player interacts with UI.

Non-interactive demo
Client
LocalScript handles the click, updates local visuals, and fires a RemoteEvent to request a change.
Example: open inventory, play sound
Server
Receives event, validates request, updates authoritative state, and optionally notifies clients back.
Example: grant purchase, save leaderstats
Common mistake
Updating leaderboards only on clients, leaving server out of sync.
Pro tip
Always validate client-sent values on the server before applying changes.
Check
Use WaitForChild when finding PlayerGui or RemoteEvents during runtime to avoid nil errors.

screens.title: Wire a Button to Game Logic — MouseButton1Click and RemoteEvents
screens.narratorSegment: Click events are the most common way players interact with UI. For mouse and touch, MouseButton1Click is the standard event on TextButton and ImageButton. In practice you use a LocalScript to listen for MouseButton1Click, and then you send an event to the server through a RemoteEvent in ReplicatedStorage. The server receives OnServerEvent with the player as the first parameter. Always validate who fired the event and the values passed in. An example flow: the client requests a purchase; the server checks the player's balance and item availability, deducts the cost, and updates the player's leaderstats before telling the client to show a confirmation. A common misconception is trusting client-side checks for affordability. If you accept client-sent prices without server validation, players can cheat. Another common mistake is placing the RemoteEvent under StarterGui—put it in ReplicatedStorage so both client and server can access the same object reliably. When wiring UI: use WaitForChild to find the event, debounce repeated clicks on the client to avoid duplicated requests, and always handle nil cases on the server. Try a short pattern: client fires RemoteEvent, server validates, server updates, server fires back or updates replicated leaderstats. That simple contract keeps UI responsive and secure.

keyIdea.title: Client asks, server authorizes
keyIdea.text: Use MouseButton1Click for UI, send the request via RemoteEvent, and always validate on the server before changing authoritative state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Button → RemoteEvent
Client-side

LocalScript Example

This LocalScript sits inside the TextButton and fires a RemoteEvent to request an action.

<!-- LocalScript inside TextButton -->
local button = script.Parent
local rep = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local addScore = rep:WaitForChild("AddScoreEvent")

button.MouseButton1Click:Connect(function()
  -- Prevent spam
  button.AutoButtonColor = false
  addScore:FireServer() -- request server to add points
  task.delay(0.2, function() button.AutoButtonColor = true end)
end)
Tip
Debounce clicks to avoid duplicate server events.
Mnemonic
Client requests, server checks, server acts.
Server-side

Server validation

OnServerEvent receives the player as first arg. Validate everything and update server state or leaderstats.

<!-- Script in ServerScriptService -->
local rep = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local addScore = rep:WaitForChild("AddScoreEvent")

addScore.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player)
  -- Validate and apply change
  if not player or not player:IsA("Player") then return end
  -- Example: add 10 points to leaderstats safely
  local stats = player:FindFirstChild("leaderstats")
  if stats and stats:FindFirstChild("Score") then
    stats.Score.Value = stats.Score.Value + 10
  end
end)
Common mistake
Trusting client-sent values as-is instead of validating on the server.
Check your work
Log received requests during development to confirm expected arguments and sender identity.

screens.title: Build a Responsive HUD: Health, Score, and a Shop Button
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical HUD you can build right now: a top bar that shows Health and Score, plus a Shop button that toggles a centered panel. Start by adding a ScreenGui named PlayerHUD into StarterGui so Roblox copies it into every player's PlayerGui when they join. Inside PlayerHUD create a Frame named TopBarFrame with AnchorPoint set to 0.5,0 and Position at UDim2. new(0.5, 0, 0, 0). Use Size UDim2. new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0) to make it scale across devices. Inside that frame add a left-aligned TextLabel for the health display and a right-aligned TextLabel for score. Finally add a TextButton named ShopButton positioned at the bottom center using AnchorPoint 0.5,1 and Position UDim2. new(0.5,0,1,-10). For interaction, put this LocalScript inside ShopButton to toggle a ShopPanel. The script uses MouseButton1Click on the client so the panel visibility changes instantly and only for that player. Remember: UI scripts that change visibility belong in LocalScripts because they affect only that player's PlayerGui. Test in Roblox Studio using Emulated Device sizes to confirm the TopBarFrame and labels resize and stay legible. A misconception to avoid: don't try to toggle UI visibility from a server Script directly; that manipulates templates rather than a player's PlayerGui. Practice this pattern to make responsive, interactive HUDs that feel snappy and reliable.

keyIdea.title: Practical HUD pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a ScreenGui in StarterGui, scale with UDim2 Scale for responsiveness, and toggle panels with LocalScripts for immediate, per-player effects.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › HUD Example
Process

Create PlayerHUD in StarterGui

  1. Add ScreenGui named PlayerHUD to StarterGui.
  2. Add Frame named TopBarFrame and set AnchorPoint to (0.5, 0) and Position to UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0, 0).
  3. Set Size to UDim2.new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0) so it scales across screens.
  4. Add TextLabels for Health and Score; set TextScaled = true for automatic font scaling.
  5. Add TextButton ShopButton with AnchorPoint (0.5,1) and Position UDim2.new(0.5,0,1,-10).
LocalScript (Shop toggle)
<!-- LocalScript placed inside ShopButton -->
local shopButton = script.Parent
local playerGui = shopButton.Parent
local shopPanel = playerGui:WaitForChild("ShopPanel") -- create this Frame under PlayerHUD

shopButton.MouseButton1Click:Connect(function()
  shopPanel.Visible = not shopPanel.Visible
end)
Visual mockup
Health: 100
Score: 0
Shop
ShopPanel is centered and invisible by default (Visible = false).
Test
Use Emulated Device sizes in Studio to confirm scaling and legibility.
Accessibility
Keep contrast high and text large enough for small screens. Prefer TextScaled.

screens.title: Responsive tweaks: WaitForChild, minimum offsets, and device testing
screens.narratorSegment: Responsive UI design is more than choosing Scale over Offset; it is also about robust loading and graceful fallbacks. First, use WaitForChild when your script looks up objects that may be copied or created at runtime. For example, in a LocalScript use local playerGui = game. Players. LocalPlayer:WaitForChild('PlayerGui') or playerGui:WaitForChild('PlayerHUD') to avoid nil errors. Second, combine Scale with a small Offset for minimum usability: use Size = UDim2. new(0.8, 40, 0.1, 12) to let elements scale while retaining a minimum pixel size. Third, AnchorPoint makes centering predictable; an AnchorPoint of 0.5,0 keeps TopBar centered even when width changes. Test frequently using Studio's Emulated Device feature to see how UIs behave on narrow and wide screens. Watch for common pitfalls: tiny font sizes caused by using pure Offset sizes, UI anchored to the wrong corner which moves unexpectedly when resizing, and directly referencing StarterGui at runtime—remember StarterGui is a template, PlayerGui holds the live instances. Also consider event sequencing: call WaitForChild for RemoteEvents in ReplicatedStorage too, and handle cases where an expected child never appears by adding a timeout fallback. The core result: your UI should load predictably, remain legible, and be tolerant of different device sizes and network timing.

keyIdea.title: Robust responsive UI
keyIdea.text: Combine Scale for responsive layout with small Offset minimums, use AnchorPoint to anchor reliably, and use WaitForChild to avoid runtime nil errors.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Responsive & Robust
Responsive formula

Scale + Offset + AnchorPoint

Use percentage-based Scale for main sizing and a small pixel Offset to keep minimum readable sizes. AnchorPoint controls the pivot so position stays predictable across size changes.

<!-- Example properties -->
TopBarFrame.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0)
TopBarFrame.Position = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0, 0)
TopBarFrame.Size = UDim2.new(0.8, 40, 0.1, 12) -- scale with minimum offset

-- Wait for PlayerGui and RemoteEvent robustly
local rep = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local addScore = rep:WaitForChild("AddScoreEvent", 5) -- optional timeout
Device test
Use Emulated Device to test narrow, square, and wide aspect ratios frequently.
Fallback
If WaitForChild times out, show a minimal placeholder UI so the player still has essential info.
Misconception
Offset alone makes fixed-size UIs; on mobiles this causes tiny elements. Prefer Scale for main sizing.
Quick checklist
  • Use Scale for primary sizing.
  • Combine small Offset for minimum sizes.
  • Set AnchorPoint to control pivot.
  • Use WaitForChild for PlayerGui and events.
  • Test multiple Emulated Devices in Studio.

screens.title: Security, sanitization, and common UI mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: As you design HUDs, be mindful of what you reveal and how you accept input. Never display sensitive or server-only data in client-side UI, such as raw internal IDs, admin flags, or unvalidated debug logs. Players can inspect client UI and, in some cases, exploit information that should remain server-only. When accepting text from players—like a username, chat label, or custom tag—sanitize before showing it. A simple approach is to strip newline and control characters and limit length before setting TextLabel. Text. For example, replace sequences of newlines with a single space and clamp the length to a reasonable maximum. Another common mistake is putting UI manipulation code in Server Scripts that attempt to find a player's PlayerGui via game. Players. LocalPlayer: this is always nil on the server. Use RemoteEvents and LocalScripts for per-player display changes. Also avoid placing RemoteEvents in StarterGui; place them in ReplicatedStorage for consistent access. Finally, test for performance: too many UI elements with heavy nested transparency can harm rendering on low-end devices. The concrete safety checklist: sanitize any player-provided text, validate all client requests on the server, keep secret data server-only, and minimize UI complexity for performance. Closing question: what single value would you validate first when a client requests an in-game purchase?

keyIdea.title: Sanitize and validate
keyIdea.text: Never trust client input: sanitize text for display, validate transaction requests on the server, and keep sensitive data out of client UI.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Security
Comparison

Safe vs Unsafe UI data

Safe: Displayed stats, cosmetics, non-sensitive preferences. Stored or validated on server if critical.
Unsafe: Internal IDs, unvalidated server flags, raw debug logs, or direct client-side funds without server confirmation.
Sanitization example
<!-- LocalScript: sanitize before showing -->
local raw = playerInputText or ""
-- remove newlines and limit length
local clean = raw:gsub("[\r
]+"," "):sub(1, 64)
label.Text = clean
Checklist
  • Sanitize all player-provided text before display.
  • Validate purchases and rewards on the server.
  • Place RemoteEvents in ReplicatedStorage, not StarterGui.
  • Use LocalScripts for PlayerGui changes only.
  • Minimize heavy transparencies and nested frames for performance.
Why this matters
Security and performance directly affect player trust and retention. Treat UI as both presentation and a potential attack surface.

fullNarratorScript:
As you approach the final polish on a Roblox game, the way you present information and controls becomes central to player enjoyment. A good user interface does more than look nice; it communicates state, reduces confusion, and enables players to take the right action quickly. In this lesson you will learn the main building blocks of Roblox UI—ScreenGui, Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, and ImageLabel—how to organize them for clarity, and how to make them responsive across devices using UDim2 and AnchorPoint. We'll also practice a simple HUD that shows health, score, and a toggled shop panel using a local script for client-side interaction. Along the way, you will see common pitfalls such as relying only on pixel offsets or failing to group elements into Frames, and learn how to avoid them. By the end, you should be able to create modular, testable UI that adapts to different devices and gives players the information they need without clutter. Think about one interface in your favorite game and how it keeps you informed—that is the standard we aim for here.

In this chapter you'll build four practical UI skills that are core to Roblox game polish. First, you'll understand the role of UI and UX: why thoughtful layout, labels, and feedback determine whether a player stays or leaves. We will explain what qualifies as UI versus UX, and give a simple example of a health indicator that both looks good and communicates state quickly. Second, you'll identify and use core Roblox UI elements such as ScreenGui, Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, and ImageLabel. You will learn where to place these objects in the Explorer and why ScreenGui copies to each player's PlayerGui. Third, you'll implement responsive layouts with UDim2, AnchorPoint, Scale and Offset. You will practice a pattern that uses Scale for primary sizing and Offset for minimum pixel adjustments so your UI looks consistent across monitors and phones. Fourth, you will develop interactive UI and wire it to game logic with a LocalScript listening for MouseButton1Click events. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency by building a simple TopBar HUD with a toggled Shop panel.

This second objectives screen describes how you will practice and verify each skill. For the ScreenGui and Frame objective, you will add a PlayerHUD ScreenGui to StarterGui and confirm it appears under PlayerGui when a test player joins. This demonstrates the per-player cloning behavior. For responsive layouts, you will set TopBarFrame to AnchorPoint 0.5 and Size with UDim2. new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0) so it remains the same proportion on phones and desktops. For interactive UI, you will insert a TextButton named ShopButton and write a small LocalScript that toggles a ShopPanel using MouseButton1Click; test that toggling is local to the player. For UI consistency, you will audit fonts, color contrast, and spacing across the HUD. Each verification step helps you catch common mistakes such as placing UI in the wrong service, overusing pixel Offsets, or leaving interactive logic on the server. These practice steps are compact and directly tied to the capsone-style activity in this chapter.

Let’s define the difference between User Interface and User Experience and why both matter in a Roblox game. User Interface refers to the concrete elements players see and interact with: TextLabels, TextButtons, ImageLabels, Frames, and the ScreenGui container that holds them. User Experience is broader: it is the player's perception of how easy the game is to read, navigate, and interact with. In practice, a UI component like a health bar is a small part of UX: its placement, color contrast, label clarity, and animation together determine whether a player recognizes their low health in time. A concrete example: a small grey numeric health value in a corner can be a UI that fails the UX test because it is hard to scan quickly during gameplay; a bold, high-contrast bar near the top with a numeric overlay is both UI and better UX. A common misconception is to treat UX as only visual polish—UX also includes feedback timing, predictability of controls, and accessibility for different devices. To check your design, ask: can a new player find the health and shop controls within three seconds? If not, iterate until you can. This definition anchors all later screens: we will make UI elements that intentionally support better UX.

ScreenGui is the top-level container for everything a player sees as part of the screen overlay. In Roblox, you design UI inside StarterGui because the engine clones those ScreenGui objects into each player's PlayerGui when they join. That cloning behavior is the reason you can safely create a health display that updates only for a single player without affecting others. A typical architecture is: StarterGui contains a ScreenGui named PlayerHUD; PlayerHUD contains Frames such as TopBarFrame and ShopPanel; inside those Frames you place TextLabels, TextButtons, and ImageLabels. A concrete example: add PlayerHUD in StarterGui, then join Play mode and inspect PlayerGui in Explorer to see the copy. A common mistake is trying to update StarterGui at runtime from a server script to change a player's display; those changes affect the template and not the already cloned PlayerGui instances. If you must change live UIs for connected players, either modify their PlayerGui or use RemoteEvents to instruct clients to update their local UI. Always prefer LocalScripts for client-side UI behavior because LocalScripts have access to LocalPlayer and run smoothly on the client. For verification, create a small ScreenGui with a TextLabel that shows the player's name using a LocalScript and see it appear per-player.

Frames are the basic containers you will use to group related UI elements. Think of Frames as panels: they provide a background, a local coordinate space, and a place to apply layout rules. When you put health and score elements inside a TopBarFrame, you can move, scale, or set visibility for the whole group with one property change. That modularity makes it easier to show or hide complex UI states like opening an inventory or toggling a shop panel. A concrete practice: create a TopBarFrame with AnchorPoint set to 0.5 on the X axis and UDim2. new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0) for Size. Inside it, place HealthLabel and ScoreLabel and set their AnchorPoints so alignment remains stable. A common error is placing many elements directly under ScreenGui without Frames, which leads to messy hierarchies and fragile scripts. Another useful technique is to use simple layout objects like UIListLayout or UIPadding inside Frames to maintain spacing when the screen size changes. For example, UIListLayout can ensure buttons stack and scale predictably when the frame resizes. End with this mental check: if you need to toggle, move, or style a set of elements together, put them in a Frame first.

Roblox provides simple building blocks: TextLabel for static text, TextButton for clickable text-based controls, ImageLabel for non-interactive images, and ImageButton when the image should be clickable. Choose the right element to match both behavior and accessibility. For example, use TextLabel for a persistent 'Health:' label. Use TextButton for an interactive 'Shop' control that players click to open a panel. An ImageLabel is great for icons such as a heart or coin, but if the icon should open an inventory, use an ImageButton instead. A concrete design decision: prefer readable fonts and sufficient text size. The chapter recommends TextScaled and a bold font for score and health numbers so they remain legible on small devices. A common beginner mistake is mixing too many styles—different fonts, colors, and button shapes—that makes interactive elements indistinguishable from decorative ones. Maintain consistent visual feedback for interactive elements: slightly darker background on pressed state or a small scale animation improves clarity. Finally, avoid placing sensitive information like server debug text in visible labels. Sanitize any player-supplied text before showing it in TextLabels to prevent confusion or exploitation. As you design, ask whether each element is decorative, informative, or interactive; pick the UI object type that reflects that role.

One of the most important technical skills for Roblox UI is mastering UDim2, which combines Scale and Offset to control both size and position. Scale values are fractions of the parent size and make elements resize proportionally. Offset values are fixed pixels used for fine-tuning. A robust pattern is to use Scale for primary sizing and Offset for small adjustments like minimum padding. For example, a TopBarFrame with Size set to UDim2. new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0) will occupy 80 percent of the screen width and 10 percent of the height on any device. AnchorPoint changes the reference point used when positioning an element. By default, position is relative to the top-left corner; setting AnchorPoint to Vector2. new(0.5, 0.5) makes the element center around its assigned Position, which simplifies centering and rotation. A common misconception is that Offset alone is sufficient; a 100-pixel wide button that looks fine on a desktop will be tiny on a phone. To test responsiveness, use Roblox Studio's emulated devices or resize the play window. Below is a concrete code example that demonstrates creating a centered play button that remains 80 percent wide using AnchorPoint and UDim2. Practice by changing Scale and observing how the UI adapts. Final takeaway: prefer Scale for major layout and AnchorPoint for predictable pivots, reserving Offset for minimum pixel spacing.

When you build in-game UI, choosing where code runs is one of the most important architecture decisions. A LocalScript runs on the player's device and can update that player's ScreenGui directly. This makes LocalScripts ideal for animations, button handling, and immediate visual feedback. A Server Script runs on the server and controls authoritative game state—things like awarding currency, changing global timers, or updating leaderboards. If you put UI-only code on the server, you either can't directly affect a single player's PlayerGui, or you create lag and security issues. Conversely, putting sensitive logic—like awarding points—only in a LocalScript lets a player spoof results. A common pattern is: LocalScript detects a button click and fires a RemoteEvent to the server; the server validates, updates authoritative state, and informs clients back. Example: the client fires a request to open a shop; the server checks whether purchases are allowed and updates the player's saved balance. Remember to test for nil values and use WaitForChild when querying PlayerGui or replicated objects. A quick misconception check: LocalScripts are not weak—use them for UI—but they are not authoritative. Your takeaway: separate presentation (LocalScript) from game authority (Server Script) and use RemoteEvents to bridge them.

Click events are the most common way players interact with UI. For mouse and touch, MouseButton1Click is the standard event on TextButton and ImageButton. In practice you use a LocalScript to listen for MouseButton1Click, and then you send an event to the server through a RemoteEvent in ReplicatedStorage. The server receives OnServerEvent with the player as the first parameter. Always validate who fired the event and the values passed in. An example flow: the client requests a purchase; the server checks the player's balance and item availability, deducts the cost, and updates the player's leaderstats before telling the client to show a confirmation. A common misconception is trusting client-side checks for affordability. If you accept client-sent prices without server validation, players can cheat. Another common mistake is placing the RemoteEvent under StarterGui—put it in ReplicatedStorage so both client and server can access the same object reliably. When wiring UI: use WaitForChild to find the event, debounce repeated clicks on the client to avoid duplicated requests, and always handle nil cases on the server. Try a short pattern: client fires RemoteEvent, server validates, server updates, server fires back or updates replicated leaderstats. That simple contract keeps UI responsive and secure.

Let's walk through a practical HUD you can build right now: a top bar that shows Health and Score, plus a Shop button that toggles a centered panel. Start by adding a ScreenGui named PlayerHUD into StarterGui so Roblox copies it into every player's PlayerGui when they join. Inside PlayerHUD create a Frame named TopBarFrame with AnchorPoint set to 0.5,0 and Position at UDim2. new(0.5, 0, 0, 0). Use Size UDim2. new(0.8, 0, 0.1, 0) to make it scale across devices. Inside that frame add a left-aligned TextLabel for the health display and a right-aligned TextLabel for score. Finally add a TextButton named ShopButton positioned at the bottom center using AnchorPoint 0.5,1 and Position UDim2. new(0.5,0,1,-10). For interaction, put this LocalScript inside ShopButton to toggle a ShopPanel. The script uses MouseButton1Click on the client so the panel visibility changes instantly and only for that player. Remember: UI scripts that change visibility belong in LocalScripts because they affect only that player's PlayerGui. Test in Roblox Studio using Emulated Device sizes to confirm the TopBarFrame and labels resize and stay legible. A misconception to avoid: don't try to toggle UI visibility from a server Script directly; that manipulates templates rather than a player's PlayerGui. Practice this pattern to make responsive, interactive HUDs that feel snappy and reliable.

Responsive UI design is more than choosing Scale over Offset; it is also about robust loading and graceful fallbacks. First, use WaitForChild when your script looks up objects that may be copied or created at runtime. For example, in a LocalScript use local playerGui = game. Players. LocalPlayer:WaitForChild('PlayerGui') or playerGui:WaitForChild('PlayerHUD') to avoid nil errors. Second, combine Scale with a small Offset for minimum usability: use Size = UDim2. new(0.8, 40, 0.1, 12) to let elements scale while retaining a minimum pixel size. Third, AnchorPoint makes centering predictable; an AnchorPoint of 0.5,0 keeps TopBar centered even when width changes. Test frequently using Studio's Emulated Device feature to see how UIs behave on narrow and wide screens. Watch for common pitfalls: tiny font sizes caused by using pure Offset sizes, UI anchored to the wrong corner which moves unexpectedly when resizing, and directly referencing StarterGui at runtime—remember StarterGui is a template, PlayerGui holds the live instances. Also consider event sequencing: call WaitForChild for RemoteEvents in ReplicatedStorage too, and handle cases where an expected child never appears by adding a timeout fallback. The core result: your UI should load predictably, remain legible, and be tolerant of different device sizes and network timing.

As you design HUDs, be mindful of what you reveal and how you accept input. Never display sensitive or server-only data in client-side UI, such as raw internal IDs, admin flags, or unvalidated debug logs. Players can inspect client UI and, in some cases, exploit information that should remain server-only. When accepting text from players—like a username, chat label, or custom tag—sanitize before showing it. A simple approach is to strip newline and control characters and limit length before setting TextLabel. Text. For example, replace sequences of newlines with a single space and clamp the length to a reasonable maximum. Another common mistake is putting UI manipulation code in Server Scripts that attempt to find a player's PlayerGui via game. Players. LocalPlayer: this is always nil on the server. Use RemoteEvents and LocalScripts for per-player display changes. Also avoid placing RemoteEvents in StarterGui; place them in ReplicatedStorage for consistent access. Finally, test for performance: too many UI elements with heavy nested transparency can harm rendering on low-end devices. The concrete safety checklist: sanitize any player-provided text, validate all client requests on the server, keep secret data server-only, and minimize UI complexity for performance. Closing question: what single value would you validate first when a client requests an in-game purchase?

These short concept cards summarize the most important ideas from this chapter. Keep LocalScripts for presentation, Server Scripts for authority, and use RemoteEvents as a validated bridge. Prefer Scale in UDim2 for responsiveness and use AnchorPoint to set stable pivots; combine a small Offset value when you need minimum pixel sizes. Organize elements under Frames and ScreenGui so each player gets an isolated PlayerGui instance, and always test using Studio's Emulated Device settings. Sanitize text from players and never rely solely on client-side checks for important game state. These habits keep your HUDs readable, reliable, and secure. As a final reflective question: which validation should always run on the server before granting any in-game resource?
